who: Reed Steiner, Ella Hannon, and Brent Hall
form: Abstract: This paper presents a spílex̣m (narrative) as told by c̓úʔsinek (Marty Aspinall) in nɬeʔkepmxcín (“Thompson River Salish”, ISO 639-3: thp). The story recalls an encounter between her qéck (older brother) and a malicious spirit that took the form of their mother. c̓úʔsinek’s story is presented in the original nɬeʔkepmxcín, and accompanied by c̓úʔsinek’s semeʔcín (English) translation and a morpheme-by-morpheme gloss by Reed Steiner, Ella Hannon, and Brent Hall. We hope that publishing c̓úʔsinek’s story and accompanying materials will be useful for nɬeʔkepmxcín speakers and learners, as well as linguists.

form: nɬeʔkepmxcín (a.k.a. Nlaka’pamux, “Thompson River Salish”, ISO 639-3: thp) is a Northern Interior Salish language with about 100 fluent speakers (Gessner et al. 2023). It is primarily spoken along the Fraser and Thompson rivers: up the Fraser from the lower Fraser River Canyon toward Lillooet, up the Thompson from where it meets the Fraser toward Ashcroft, and along the Nicola River from where it meets the Thompson to just past Nicola Lake (Thompson and Thompson 1996: ix).

form: Several regional dialects have been identified (see Thompson and Thompson 1996: xxv-xxvii). The Spuzzum dialect has the most documentation, as it is the primary object of study of Thompson and Thompson's grammar (1992) and dictionary (1996). There is also significant documentation on the ƛ̓q̓mcín (Lytton) dialect, which features heavily in work by Koch (2004, 2005, 2006a-c, 2007a-c, 2008, 2009, 2010, 2011a-c, 2012, 2013a-b, 2015), as well as more recent literature (Hall and Phillips 2024, Givens and Hall 2023, Hall 2023, Reid 2023). Documentation on the scwexmxcín (Nicola Valley) dialect and the closely related c̓eɬétkʷu (Coldwater) dialect has been increasing since 2023 (Hannon 2025, kʷaɬtèzetkʷ et al. 2024, Hannon 2024a-b, Hannon et al. 2023, Hannon & Smith 2023, Pirbaluti 2023).

form: This spíləx̣m (‘narrative’) is told by c̓úʔsinek in the scwew̓xmxcín dialect of nɬeʔkepmxcín. In this story, c̓úʔsinek recalls an encounter between her qéck ‘older brother’ and a malicious spirit, which looked and sounded like their mother. Despite their mother’s instructions to stay put, c̓úʔsinek’s qéck followed the spirit's voice into the bush.

form: c̓úʔsinek shares this story now as a warning. She warns that if one does not listen to their elders, and if one does not take the proper precautions before going out on the land, then even today the land may take them. She hopes that the story will remind young people not to neglect their teachings when they go out on the land, and that their traditional practices and preparations exist for a good reason.

form: In September of 2024, c̓úʔsinek recorded the story on her iPhone, and sent Steiner an .m4a file. The story was transcribed by Steiner and Hannon, using the North American Phonetic Alphabet (NAPA) as used by Thompson and Thompson (1992, 1996). Most words were spelled as in the dictionary (Thompson and Thomspon 1996), except where c̓úʔsinek's pronunciation differed significantly. False starts, fluency breaks, and repeated segments are not transcribed, per c̓úʔsinek's request. No punctuation or capitalization is used, following the preferences of both c̓úʔsinek and many members of the broader speech community (Na'zinek Mandy Jimmie, p.c.). A colon indicates rhetorical lengthening. For readability, each sentence is written on a separate line.
gloss: THE TRANSCRIPTION IS IN NAPA AS THOMPSON AND THOMPSON USE IT, WITH NO PUNCTUATION OR CAPITALS, AND A COLON MARKS RHETORICAL LENGTHENING. c̓úʔsinek's is written here with the straight ASCII apostrophe

form: All English translations are in c̓úʔsinek's own words. To collect translations, Steiner met with c̓úʔsinek over Zoom, played a segment of audio, and asked for its meaning in English. Audio was repeated as many times as necessary. These meetings occurred regularly from September to late October 2024, with occasional follow-up meetings through June 2025. c̓úʔsinek often made additional comments about the story during these meetings; those comments that pertain to the transcription and interpretation have been included in the footnotes. Occasionally, c̓úʔsinek chose to replace a word or phrase with one that differs from the recording, for the sake of clarity or precision.
